How To Rob A Bank.review: David Leitch’s high-energy heist film has a lively premise and plenty of kinetic action, but its anti-capitalist satire is undercut by thinly drawn characters, dated internet humour and a story that rarely gives its robbers meaningful consequences. It can be a diverting, throwaway caper, yet it never turns its political anger into the urgency or emotional force it promises.

Whispers In The Woods.review: Filmmaker Vincent Munier explores the forests of the Vosges with his father and son in a visually ravishing, quietly moving portrait of the natural world. Its patient observation and tender sense of family make it both an immersive wildlife film and a thoughtful reflection on the passing of knowledge between generations.

Fjord.review: An austere, slow-burning drama turns a family dispute into an unsettling clash of religious conviction, cultural difference and state power. Its finely balanced performances and refusal to settle the argument make it provocative and absorbing, though the unresolved story and deliberate pace can feel frustrating rather than revelatory.

Marie Antoinette (20th Anniversary 4K Re.review: Sofia Coppola’s stylised portrait of the young queen returns in a sumptuous 4K restoration, pairing lavish period imagery with anachronistic pop music. Kirsten Dunst brings an intimate vulnerability to the role, while the film’s distinctive visual and musical choices give this unconventional costume drama its enduring appeal.

The Man Who Fell To Earth (50th Annivers.review: Nicolas Roeg’s strange, visually audacious science-fiction film remains a haunting portrait of alienation and media-saturated modern life, centred on David Bowie’s otherworldly performance. Its warnings about technology and human disconnection feel strikingly current, while its fragmented, deliberately unsettling style remains an essential part of its singular atmosphere.

Give Me The Ball!.review: This engaging portrait of Billie Jean King connects her sporting dominance with her fight for equal pay and wider social change. Lively archive footage and candid reflection give the documentary real energy, while its account of King’s advocacy makes clear how far her influence extended beyond the tennis court.

100 Sunset.review: Set within Toronto’s Tibetan community, this quiet, elusive drama follows a withdrawn teenager whose petty theft draws her into the lives of her neighbours. Its dreamlike, disorientating style can be deliberately uncomfortable, but that very strangeness gives the film a distinctive and lingering power.

Ebenezer.review: Ti West gives A Christmas Carol a gloomy, horror-tinged makeover with lavish period detail and a few effective ghostly shocks, but the familiar story is played too straight to feel newly revealing. Johnny Depp’s exaggerated, theatrical Scrooge can be amusingly offbeat yet also tips into mannered caricature, leaving the film visually accomplished but emotionally thin.

Being Heumann.review: Ruth Madeley gives a forceful, sympathetic performance as disability-rights campaigner Judy Heumann in this account of the 1977 Section 504 occupation. The film brings heartfelt energy to a remarkable story of collective activism, even if familiar biopic conventions and lightly drawn supporting characters sometimes blunt its impact.

The Mosquito Bowl.review: Peter Berg’s Pacific war drama delivers brutal, well-staged battle sequences and clear technical polish, but the four football-playing Marines remain thinly sketched and the episodic story struggles to build emotional weight. Its echoes of Saving Private Ryan are unmistakable, yet the film lacks that film’s coherence and human depth.

Prima Facie.review: Cynthia Erivo gives a fierce, commanding central performance that keeps this courtroom drama emotionally charged, especially in its depiction of reporting sexual assault and confronting a legal system stacked against complainants. The move from a single stage monologue to conventional screen storytelling sometimes blunts the original’s immediacy, but its moral urgency and lead performance remain potent.

1 IN 2.review: David Wilkinson turns the camera on his own stage-four bowel cancer treatment while investigating the rise of the disease among younger people. The result is a compassionate, candid and often humorous documentary that gives patients and NHS staff a voice while making a clear case for greater awareness of symptoms and screening.

A FOX UNDER A PINK MOON.review: Filmed over five years on a smartphone, this striking documentary follows Afghan teenager Soraya Akhlaghi’s repeated attempts to escape Iran and join her mother in Austria. Its intimate, often harrowing account is given added emotional depth by the vivid drawings and animations through which Soraya expresses her hopes and fears.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping.synopsis: A prequel set 24 years before the original Hunger Games, following young Haymitch Abernathy as he is drawn into the 50th Hunger Games.

A Talent For Murder.review: Helen Mirren relishes the role of a fictionalised Patricia Highsmith in this witty, literary chamber thriller, sparring with an ambitious young editor who hopes to coax one last Ripley novel from her. The performances and sharp dialogue make it an enjoyable watch, but its central mystery lacks the menace and tension of Highsmith’s best work.

Josephine.review: A quietly devastating drama about an eight-year-old girl struggling to process a sexual assault she witnesses, anchored by a remarkable performance from young Mason Reeves. Its sensitive attention to the child’s fear and the strain on her family is powerful, though some of the film’s procedural turns and visual choices feel more contrived than convincing.

Filipinana.review: A visually sumptuous, quietly unsettling debut turns an elite Manila golf club into a microcosm of class privilege, exploitation and colonial power. Its deliberate pacing and elusive storytelling demand patience, but the carefully composed images and growing sense of menace give the satire a lasting bite.

You Can See Everything.review: This audacious documentary-hybrid turns the story of Elizabeth Holmes into a gripping, often surreal study of performance, deception and the manufacture of reality. Nathan Fielder’s unsettling methods and the film’s unexpected shifts make it as provocative as it is entertaining, although its deliberate blurring of fact and fiction leaves plenty of questions hanging.

Focker-In-Law.synopsis: Greg Focker's son brings his girlfriend home to meet the family, prompting fresh anxieties when he announces plans to propose.

Buddy.synopsis: A dark horror-comedy about a children’s television performer whose cheerful on-screen persona gives way to something far more disturbing.

Minotaur.synopsis: In contemporary Russia, a company executive's marriage and career unravel as he faces pressure to supply employees for military conscription.

Disney's Hexed.synopsis: An unconventional teenager discovers magical powers and is swept into a hidden witch realm, where she and her cautious mother uncover family secrets.

Ghost Soldier.synopsis: An action thriller following a soldier caught in a dangerous mission behind enemy lines.

The Cat In The Hat.synopsis: The mischievous Cat is sent on a mission to cheer up siblings Gabby and Sebastian, but his talent for chaos puts his magical hat and his future at risk.

Violent Night 2.synopsis: When Santa loses his magic, he must help a mall community threatened by a ruthless gangster and rediscover the meaning of Christmas.

Behemoth!.synopsis: A gifted cellist returns to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road, confronting the life and music he left behind.

Magellan.synopsis: The 16th-century Portuguese navigator leads an arduous expedition to the East, where his ambitions turn towards conquest and religious conversion.

Nuisance Bear.synopsis: A polar bear's traditional migration brings it into conflict with people in the Canadian Arctic, exposing the uneasy overlap between wildlife and human communities.

I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.synopsis: A drama exploring memory, loss and the changing urban landscape.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping.review: This expansive prequel gives Haymitch’s origins a brutal, emotionally charged backstory, with a strong central performance and an impressive ensemble. Its familiar franchise machinery and overextended plotting can make it feel like another instalment rather than a fresh reinvention, but it remains a substantial, often gripping return to Panem.

Disney’s Hexed.synopsis: An unconventional teenager discovers magical powers and is swept into a hidden witch realm, where she and her cautious mother uncover family secrets.

ChaO.synopsis: In a future where humans and mermaids uneasily coexist, an engineer’s life is upended when a mermaid princess unexpectedly proposes marriage.

Vidudala.synopsis: Two army officers and close friends find their skills tested when they are drawn into a series of national-defence crises.

Mega158.synopsis: A quiet shrimp-farm supervisor’s life takes a dangerous turn when a discovery at work reveals that the business is hiding a cache of weapons.

Kaaka.synopsis: A quiet shrimp-farm supervisor’s life takes a dangerous turn when a discovery at work reveals that the business is hiding a cache of weapons.

George Krish.synopsis: A Telugu-language science-fiction comedy starring Sharwanand in the contrasting roles of George and Krish.

American Doctor.review: This harrowing documentary follows three American doctors working in Gaza’s overwhelmed hospitals, then traces their efforts to make the suffering they witnessed heard back home. Its unflinching images are difficult to watch, but the doctors’ commitment and the film’s clear-eyed account of medical work under bombardment give it considerable urgency and emotional force.

Heysel 85.review: This dramatisation of the 1985 Heysel Stadium disaster gives a tense, human perspective on the chaos surrounding the Liverpool–Juventus European Cup final. Its staging conveys the scale of the tragedy, but a thin script, uneven performances and limited resources struggle to do justice to the historical weight of the events.

Steps.review: This lively Cinderella reworking gives the supposedly wicked stepsisters their own story, with spirited voice performances and enough comic energy to keep the adventure moving. The plot becomes crowded with subplots and familiar fairytale reversals, while the animation lacks a distinctive look, but its humour and pace make it a cheerful family diversion.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.review: Mahershala Ali gives a deeply felt performance as a widowed Muslim hitman trying to reconcile his violent work with the demands of fatherhood and faith. The film’s vivid, often brutal action is matched by an unexpectedly tender family drama, though its deliberately strange tone and crowded religious themes make for an unsettling rather than straightforwardly entertaining experience.

The Match.synopsis: A documentary revisits the 1986 Argentina–England World Cup quarter-final, examining how the match became a flashpoint for tensions between the two nations.

CBeebies Panto 2026: Treasure Island.synopsis: A filmed family pantomime follows Jim and his dad Bertie on a swashbuckling treasure hunt, with pirates, songs, comedy and familiar CBeebies performers.

70 Syaal.synopsis: A man returns with his family to his ancestral village in Punjab to bring peace to his dying father, but their homecoming awakens a decades-old supernatural curse that threatens his wife and newborn child.

Arthur Christmas (15th Anniversary).synopsis: When Santa's high-tech operation misses one child, his youngest son Arthur sets out on a frantic Christmas Eve mission to deliver the forgotten present before morning.

Sathyavan Savithri.synopsis: A young lawyer takes on the case of her husband, whom she believes has been wrongly convicted of murder, and finds herself opposed in court by her own mentor.
